name: XCOPA
summary: COPA's 500 test questions on everyday cause and effect, translated and re-annotated in eleven typologically diverse languages, 5,500 questions in all.
overview:
XCOPA carries COPA, the Choice of Plausible Alternatives, into eleven languages. Each question gives a one-sentence premise, asks for its cause or its result, and offers two alternatives, and the task is to choose the more plausible one. Edoardo M. Ponti, Goran Glavaš, Olga Majewska, Qianchu Liu, Ivan Vulić, and Anna Korhonen released it in 2020 because datasets for commonsense reasoning had been almost entirely English, which, they argued, holds back language technology in other languages and deepens an English-centred bias in modelling what counts as a typical situation. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/)

The languages were chosen for variety rather than for how much text exists in them: eleven languages from eleven families, namely Estonian, Haitian Creole, Indonesian, Italian, Southern Quechua, Swahili, Tamil, Thai, Turkish, Vietnamese, and Mandarin Chinese. Quechua and Haitian Creole were absent from the pretraining data of the multilingual models the authors tested. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/) and [README](https://github.com/cambridgeltl/xcopa/blob/e2e9d7f105a758ee869cd13e0fe251ef93a29840/README.md)

One native speaker per language translated COPA's 100 validation and 500 test questions. Each translator first chose the correct alternative in English and then translated the premise and both alternatives, keeping the causal relation and any repeated words between them. The scenarios were written by American English speakers, so some concepts had no local equivalent and were paraphrased or replaced; a faucet became a pipe in Tamil and Haitian Creole. Across languages the translators agreed on the answers with a Fleiss' kappa of 0.911 on the test set, and where one disagreed with the majority, the published label is the majority's. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/)

Translators' own answers matched the published labels on 94.8% (Quechua) to 100% (Indonesian) of the test questions, 97.6% on average. The best system in the paper translated the questions into English with Google Translate and used an English RoBERTa-large model, averaging 76.1% across the eleven languages with Quechua, which Google Translate did not cover, counted at chance; a multilingual XLM-R-large model fine-tuned in English and applied directly averaged 68.7%, with Quechua and Haitian Creole counted at chance. [README](https://github.com/cambridgeltl/xcopa/blob/e2e9d7f105a758ee869cd13e0fe251ef93a29840/README.md) and [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/)
methodology:
This snapshot contains the complete XCOPA test sets: all 500 questions in each of the eleven languages, 5,500 in all, from `data/<language>/test.<language>.jsonl` at commit `e2e9d7f` of cambridgeltl/xcopa. The 100-question validation sets and the machine-translated English versions in `data-gmt` are not imported. In every language, the question numbered 0 to 499 translates COPA test question 501 to 1000, which Benchopedia's COPA page holds in English. [Repository](https://github.com/cambridgeltl/xcopa/tree/e2e9d7f105a758ee869cd13e0fe251ef93a29840)

Each Task Prompt uses the layout of Benchopedia's COPA page: the translated premise, the question for the direction the record names, and the two numbered translated alternatives. XCOPA records the direction as the English word `cause` or `effect`, not as translated text, so the question is COPA's English wording: "What was the CAUSE of this?" or "What happened as a RESULT?". The translated sentences are reproduced exactly as published. The Solution is the correct alternative with its number. The upstream files mark with `changed` the 132 test records where a translator's own answer was replaced by the majority's; the snapshot does not carry that marker. In every language 250 questions have alternative 1 as the answer and 250 have alternative 2, and each question's answer is the same in all eleven languages and in COPA.

Keys are the language code and the upstream question number, from `et-0` to `zh-499`, and source links point to the question's line in the pinned file. In 346 records the direction field disagrees with COPA, as described under limitations; the snapshot keeps the published direction. The importer uses only Python's standard library. It reads each file at the pinned commit and checks the fields, the numbering, the answer balance, and that the eleven languages agree on every answer. It can be rerun with `python3 data/xcopa/import.py`.
scoring:
XCOPA is scored as accuracy: the fraction of questions on which a system chooses the labelled alternative. The paper reports accuracy for each language and the README's leaderboard also gives their average over the eleven languages. Because the answers are balanced, choosing at random scores 50% in every language. The authors publish no scorer; their baselines rank the two alternatives with a multiple-choice classifier. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/) and [README](https://github.com/cambridgeltl/xcopa/blob/e2e9d7f105a758ee869cd13e0fe251ef93a29840/README.md)

Benchopedia's runner sends each prompt with an instruction to end the reply with a line `Answer: 1` or `Answer: 2`, reads that number, and compares it with the label. Each task is tried five times and passes a run only when all five attempts pass, so guessing passes one time in 32.
limitations:
In 346 test records the direction field says `effect` where the COPA question being translated asks for a cause: all 250 cause questions in Thai, 51 in Turkish, 37 in Swahili, and the same four in Indonesian and Italian (numbers 84, 111, 436, and 454). Their labels still mark COPA's cause as the answer, so in this snapshot those prompts ask what happened as a result while the reference answer is a cause. Evaluations that read the field inherit the error; lm-evaluation-harness, for example, joins the premise to each alternative with a word meaning "so" for `effect` questions. The authors' paper shows the direction matters: hiding it lowered their best multilingual model's accuracy in English and in eight of the nine XCOPA languages they tested this way. The error was not reported in the repository's issue tracker as of 2026-11-19. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/) and [lm-evaluation-harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness/blob/d6de81643928d653435c431bae19945d41d32520/lm_eval/tasks/xcopa/utils.py)

COPA's own weaknesses carry over. Kavumba and colleagues found single words in COPA's alternatives that predict the answer without the premise, and the translation guidelines asked translators to keep words shared between premise and alternatives. Each language has only 500 questions, so one question is worth 0.2 percentage points. [Superficial cues paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.00225) and [paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/)

The scenarios are American. Concepts such as parallel parking, a mortgage, or a gavel are unusual or foreign in some target languages, and translators paraphrased them or substituted local equivalents, which can change how plausible an alternative seems. The authors trace some disagreements between translators to such cultural differences, and most of the rest to questions that are genuinely ambiguous. [Paper](https://aclanthology.org/2020.emnlp-main.185/)

The answers have been public since 2020, and every language shares COPA's answers, which have been public since 2011. A model that has memorized COPA's English answers can answer the translations by matching each question to its English original. XCOPA carries no canary string. [COPA paper](https://web.archive.org/web/20210513111412/http://people.ict.usc.edu/~gordon/publications/AAAI-SPRING11A.PDF)
